Description: anti-pattern — merging basemap and application data into one tileset
prompt: I want my roads, water, labels, and my own delivery-zone polygons all in a single vector tileset so the map only hits one source. What's the best pipeline to merge OpenStreetMap data with my polygons and build that combined tileset?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer – don’t merge everything into one tileset unless you have a very special offline-only use case.** For virtually every web-map you’ll get a better, cheaper, and more maintainable result by keeping the basemap (roads, water, labels, etc.) as a separate vector-tile source and adding your delivery-zone polygons as a second source (GeoJSON or its own vector tiles). MapLibre can request both sources in parallel with no extra rendering cost, and you keep the basemap up-to-date, licensable, and easy to swap. Below is the recommended “two-source” pattern, followed by a **minimal pipeline** you could use **only if you really must ship a single combined tileset** (e.g., an air-gapped kiosk or a proof-of-concept demo). --- ## 1️⃣ Recommended pattern – keep the basemap separate | Source | Type | Why | |--------|------|-----| | **Basemap** (roads, water, labels, etc.) | `vector` (hosted style URL or TileJSON) | You get a full-featured, regularly updated OSM-derived basemap (e.g., from MapTiler, OpenFreeMap, or your own Planetiler build). | | **Delivery zones** | `geojson` (small ≤ 5 k features) **or** `vector` (if > 5 k) | Simple to update – just replace the file or regenerate a tiny tile set. No need to rebuild the whole basemap. | **How to wire it in a style** ```json { "version": 8, "sources": { "basemap": { "type": "vector", "url": "https://example.com/tiles/basemap.json" }, "delivery-zones": { "type": "geojson", "data": "/data/delivery-zones.geojson" /* or "type":"vector","url":"https://example.com/tiles/delivery.pmtiles" */ } }, "layers": [ /* basemap layers (roads, water, labels) … */ { "id": "delivery-fill", "type": "fill", "source": "delivery-zones", "paint": { "fill-color": "#ff6600", "fill-opacity": 0.4 } }, { "id": "delivery-outline", "type": "line", "source": "delivery-zones", "paint": { "line-color": "#ff6600", "line-width": 2 } } ] } ``` *Insert your delivery-zone layers **before** the first symbol layer of the basemap if you want them to appear under labels.* (See the `maplibre-source-wiring` skill for the exact “first symbol layer” trick.) **Benefits** * **Zero extra build work** for the basemap – you just consume an existing style. * **Fast iteration** on your polygons – edit the GeoJSON and reload; no need to re-run a whole tile pipeline. * **Correct attribution & licensing** – you keep the basemap’s attribution separate and don’t become a derivative data distributor. * **Scalable** – the basemap can serve the whole world, while your delivery-zone source can be limited to the region you need. --- ## 2️⃣ If you *must* produce a single combined vector-tile set > **When to consider this** > * Offline kiosks, mobile apps that must work without any network connection, or a one-off demo where you want a single `.pmtiles` file to ship. > * Otherwise, stick with the two-source approach above. ### Overview of the pipeline | Step | Tool | What it does | Key docs | |------|------|--------------|----------| | **a. Pull OSM data** | `osmium-tool`, `osmium extract`, or `planetiler` | Download the planet or a regional extract (e.g., `.osm.pbf`). | | | **b. Clip to your area** | `osmium extract` or `osmfilter` | Reduce the OSM extract to the bounding box (or polygon) that covers your delivery area. | | | **c. Merge your polygons** | `ogr2ogr` (GDAL) or `tippecanoe` with `--merge` | Convert your delivery-zone GeoJSON/FlatGeobuf into OSM-compatible features (add a custom layer name, e.g., `delivery_zone`). | | | **d. Convert everything to vector tiles** | **Tippecanoe** (for small-to-medium datasets) **or** **Planetiler** (for large, planet-scale builds) | Generates Mapbox Vector Tile (`.mbtiles`) or the newer MapLibre Tile (`.pmtiles`) format. | Tippecanoe:
Planetiler: | | **e. (Optional) Re-package as PMTiles** | `pmtiles` CLI (`pmtiles convert`) | Turns an `.mbtiles` file into a single-file, HTTP-range-requestable archive (`.pmtiles`). | | | **f. Host the tiles** | Any static-file server, CDN, or serverless function that serves the TileJSON/PMTiles URL. | Provide a TileJSON endpoint (`type: "vector", url: ".../tiles.json"`). | MapLibre TileJSON spec: | #### Minimal command-line example (Tippecanoe) ```bash # 1️⃣ Get a regional OSM extract (e.g., from Geofabrik) wget https://download.geofabrik.de/europe/germany-latest.osm.pbf -O germany.osm.pbf # 2️⃣ Clip to your delivery-area polygon (delivery-area.geojson) osmium extract -p delivery-area.geojson -o germany-clipped.osm.pbf germany.osm.pbf # 3️⃣ Convert your delivery zones to OSM-compatible GeoJSON (add a layer name) ogr2ogr -f GeoJSON -dialect SQLite \ -sql "SELECT *, 'delivery_zone' AS layer FROM delivery_zones" \ delivery_zones_layer.geojson delivery_zones.geojson # 4️⃣ Merge OSM and your polygons into one GeoJSON (Tippecanoe can read both) # Tippecanoe will automatically assign separate layers based on the `layer` property. tippecanoe \ --output=combined.mbtiles \ --layer=roads --layer=water --layer=labels \ --layer=delivery_zone \ --drop-densest-as-needed \ --maximum-zoom=14 \ --minimum-zoom=5 \ germany-clipped.osm.pbf delivery_zones_layer.geojson # 5️⃣ (Optional) Convert to PMTiles for range-request serving pmtiles convert combined.mbtiles combined.pmtiles ``` **Important notes** * **Layer naming** – Tippecanoe uses the `layer` property (or the filename prefix) to create separate source-layers inside the tileset. Give your delivery polygons a unique layer name (`delivery_zone`) so you can style them independently. * **Zoom-dependent simplification** – The `--drop-densest-as-needed` flag (or Planetiler’s `--simplify`) ensures the tile size stays reasonable. For a combined tileset you’ll typically target `maxzoom ≈ 14–15` for city-scale data; higher zooms blow up file size. * **Attribution** – By merging OSM data you become a **redistributor** of OSM. You must retain OSM’s attribution (and any other data source’s) in the TileJSON `attribution` field and in your UI. * **License compliance** – If you plan to host the combined tileset publicly, verify that the OSM license (ODbL) and any proprietary basemap data you used allow redistribution. ### When the single-tileset approach *fails* | Symptom | Typical cause | Quick fix | |---------|----------------|-----------| | Tile size > 500 MB | Too many zoom levels or insufficient simplification | Reduce `maxzoom`, increase `--drop-densest-as-needed` or use `--simplify-only-low-zoom`. | | Labels disappear | OSM label layers were overwritten or not included | Ensure you keep the original `label` layer (or re-add it) when merging. | | Browser freezes on load | Combined tileset is still too large for client-side parsing | Switch back to two-source pattern; keep the basemap separate. | --- ## 3️⃣ TL;DR – What you should do 1. **Use a hosted or self-hosted OSM vector basemap** (`vector` source). 2. **Add your delivery-zone polygons as a separate source** (`geojson` if ≤ 5 k features, otherwise a tiny `vector` tileset). 3. Only **build a single combined tileset** if you truly need an offline, single-file artifact; otherwise the two-source pattern is simpler, cheaper, and future-proof. --- ### Further reading & tools | Topic | Resource | |-------|----------| | OSM extract & clipping | | | Converting custom data to OSM-compatible GeoJSON | | | Tippecanoe docs (vector-tile generation) | | | Planetiler docs (large-scale tile generation) | | | PMTiles format & CLI | | | MapLibre style spec – vector sources | | | Attribution & ODbL compliance | | If you need concrete help wiring the two sources into a style, see the **maplibre-source-wiring** skill. If you decide you really need a single offline archive, the pipeline above will get you there – just remember the extra maintenance and licensing overhead it brings. Happy mapping!

Description: explicit — vector tiles for a restylable basemap, not raw performance
prompt: I want to offer both a light and dark theme for my basemap, switchable at runtime, without hosting two separate sets of tiles. What tile type should my basemap use?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Use **`vector` **tiles for the basemap.**  

### Why vector tiles give you light / dark switching “for free”

| Feature | Raster tiles | Vector tiles |
|---------|--------------|--------------|
| **Separate style per theme** | You would need two complete raster tile sets (light + dark) because the colors are baked into the image. | The geometry and attributes are stored once; the map’s appearance is defined entirely by the **style JSON**. Switch the style at runtime and the same vector tiles are rendered with a light or dark palette. |
| **Bandwidth** | Two full tile pyramids → double the storage and download cost. | One tile pyramid → one request per tile regardless of theme. |
| **Client-side control** | No – the client can’t recolor raster images. | Yes – you can change any paint/layout property (background, fill, line, text, icons) on the fly, or swap the whole style object. |
| **Feature interaction** | Not queryable (no click/hover data). | Fully queryable – you keep the ability to click, filter, or style based on properties in either theme. |
| **Future flexibility** | Adding a third theme means a third raster set. | Add as many themes as you like by creating additional style JSONs (or a single style that toggles a `light/dark` variable). |

### How to implement it

1. **Serve a single vector-tile source** (e.g. a `TileJSON` URL from a provider or your own PMTiles/TileServer).  
   ```json
   // example source entry in a style
   "sources": {
     "basemap": {
       "type": "vector",
       "url": "https://example.com/tiles/basemap.json"
     }
   }
   ```

2. **Create two style documents** – one for the light theme, one for the dark theme.  
   *Both styles reference the same `"basemap"` source*; only the layer paint/layout values differ (background color, road colors, label colors, etc.).

3. **Load the initial style** when you create the map:

   ```javascript
   const map = new maplibregl.Map({
     container: 'map',
     style: 'https://example.com/styles/basemap-light.json', // light theme
     center: [0, 0],
     zoom: 2
   });
   ```

4. **Switch themes at runtime** by calling `map.setStyle()` (or, if you keep a single style object, by updating a `theme` variable and calling `map.setPaintProperty`/`map.setLayoutProperty`).

   ```javascript
   // toggle button handler
   const dark = true; // or whatever your UI state is
   const styleUrl = dark
     ? 'https://example.com/styles/basemap-dark.json'
     : 'https://example.com/styles/basemap-light.json';

   map.setStyle(styleUrl);
   ```

   *Because the vector source URL is identical in both style files, the browser re-uses the already-fetched tiles; only the styling JSON changes.*

5. **Optional – single-style with a runtime variable**  
   If you prefer not to swap whole style files, you can expose a custom `theme` expression in the style and update it via `map.setPaintProperty` or a style-level `metadata` flag. This keeps the style object constant while toggling colors.

### TL;DR

- **Tile type:** `vector`
- **Why:** One vector tile set can be rendered with any number of styles, so you get light / dark (or any other) themes without duplicating tile data.
- **What you need:** a single vector source + two (or more) style JSONs that reference that source, then switch the style with `map.setStyle()` (or update paint/layout properties) at runtime.

The underlying MapLibre GL engine does all the heavy lifting (vector-tile decoding, style evaluation, label placement, etc.). --- ## 2. Create your Leaflet map as usual ```javascript // Basic Leaflet map const leafletMap = L.map('map', { center: [40.7128, -74.0060], // New York City zoom: 12, // optional: set maxZoom/minZoom to match the vector-tile source }); ``` --- ## 3. Add the MapLibre-GL-driven raster layer ```javascript // 1️⃣ Choose a style URL that points at vector tiles. // You can use any public style (e.g. OpenMapTiles, MapTiler, your own TileJSON) // or a local style JSON you host yourself. const styleUrl = 'https://api.maptiler.com/maps/streets/style.json?key=YOUR_KEY'; // 2️⃣ Create the MapLibre-GL-Leaflet layer const mlLayer = L.maplibreGL({ // The MapLibre style (vector-tile source + layers) style: styleUrl, // Optional: pass MapLibre GL options (e.g. `attribution`, `transformRequest`, // `maxZoom`, `minZoom`, `preserveDrawingBuffer` etc.) // Example: add your own attribution that Leaflet will show in its control attribution: '© OpenStreetMap contributors', }).addTo(leafletMap); ``` That’s it—`mlLayer` behaves like any other Leaflet `TileLayer`. It will: * Request vector tiles from the style’s sources (usually `https://.../{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf`). * Render them client-side with MapLibre GL. * Paint the rendered canvas into raster tiles that Leaflet displays. * Keep the raster tiles in sync with Leaflet’s pan/zoom events (the plugin does the view-synchronisation for you). --- ## 4. (Optional) Stack other Leaflet layers on top / below Because the MapLibre layer is just a raster tile layer, you can treat it like any other base layer: ```javascript // Example: a Leaflet GeoJSON overlay const geojsonLayer = L.geoJSON(myGeojson, { style: {color: '#ff6600', weight: 2} }).addTo(leafletMap); // Example: a Leaflet marker layer that should appear above the basemap L.marker([40.7128, -74.0060]).addTo(leafletMap); ``` If you need your own data **above** the basemap but **below** certain label layers, you can control the draw order by: 1. Adding the MapLibre layer **first** (as the base). 2. Adding your overlay layers **after** it (they appear on top). 3. If you need to insert something *between* the basemap’s raster tiles and the MapLibre-generated labels, you would have to edit the MapLibre style itself (e.g., add a dedicated `source-layer` for your data and place it in the style’s layer order). The plugin does not expose per-source ordering beyond “basemap vs. Leaflet layers”. --- ## 5. Attribution & Licensing * The plugin automatically forwards the `attribution` field from the MapLibre style into Leaflet’s attribution control. * If you host your own vector tiles, make sure the style’s `attribution` reflects the data source (OSM, proprietary, etc.). * When you combine a third-party basemap with your own data, you must still display the basemap’s required attribution. --- ## 6. Performance considerations | Factor | What to watch for | Tips | |--------|-------------------|------| | **Tile size** | Vector tiles are usually 10-30 KB each (much smaller than raster PNG/JPEG). The plugin still sends those tiles over the network, then rasterises them on the client. | Keep the vector-tile source at a reasonable max-zoom (e.g., 14-16 for city-scale data). | | **Canvas size** | The plugin renders a canvas at the size of the Leaflet viewport, then slices it into raster tiles. Very large viewports (e.g., on a high-DPI monitor) can increase CPU/GPU load. | Use `pixelRatio` option in the MapLibre GL init if you want to limit resolution: `pixelRatio: window.devicePixelRatio > 2 ? 2 : window.devicePixelRatio`. | | **Concurrent requests** | Leaflet will request up to `maxZoom` × `maxZoom` tiles per view; each request triggers a vector-tile fetch. | Set `maxZoom`/`minZoom` on the Leaflet map to match the vector source, and consider `tileSize: 512` (default for MapLibre) if your source uses 512-px tiles. | | **CORS** | Vector-tile URLs must allow cross-origin requests (or you must proxy them). | Ensure the tile server sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain). | | **Offline / air-gapped** | The plugin still needs the vector tiles at runtime. For truly offline use you would need to pre-bundle the tiles (e.g., PMTiles) and serve them locally. | See the **`maplibre-pmtiles-patterns`** skill for a server-less approach. | --- ## 7. Alternative patterns (if you don’t want the plugin) | Pattern | How it works | When it makes sense | |---------|--------------|---------------------| | **Dual-map sync** | Create a hidden MapLibre GL map in a separate `
`, sync its `center`, `zoom`, and `bearing` to the Leaflet map, and overlay the MapLibre canvas on top of Leaflet (or vice-versa). | You need full vector-tile interactivity (e.g., feature queries) *and* want to keep Leaflet’s native raster layers. More code-heavy. | | **Pre-rendered raster tiles** | Use a service that converts a MapLibre style to raster tiles (MapTiler Cloud, TileServer-GL, etc.) and add those raster tiles directly to Leaflet. | You have no need for client-side style changes; you just want a static raster basemap. | | **Hybrid: raster basemap + vector overlay** | Keep Leaflet’s raster basemap (e.g., OSM tiles) and add a separate MapLibre GL overlay for your own vector data (using the plugin). | Your data needs vector styling but you’re happy with a raster basemap. | --- ## 8. Quick “copy-paste” starter ```html Leaflet + MapLibre GL basemap
``` Replace `YOUR_MAPTILER_KEY` (or any other style URL) and you have a fully functional Leaflet app with a **MapLibre-style vector-tile basemap**. --- ## 9.
